passage: Monday: Yamini, four, counted the steps up to her Ajji Urmila's flat: "One, two, three, seven, ten!" and ran up two at a time. Thursday: Ajji put laddoos on two plates. Yamini touched each one as she counted: "One, two, three, four." She did the other plate: "One, two." The next Sunday: Ajji put out the plates again. Yamini didn't count at all. She pointed. "That one has more. I want that one." Ajji laughed and gave her the smaller plate first.

qa.q: What did Yamini touch as she counted on Thursday?
qa.a: Each laddoo on the plates.

qa.q: What might Yamini have wanted when she pointed at the bigger plate?
qa.a: She wanted the plate with more laddoos and seemed confident she could tell without counting.

qa.q: How could Ajji Urmila keep building Yamini's counting?
qa.a: Keep giving small everyday chances to count and compare, like steps, laddoos or shoes, and let her check by touching.

qa.q: How might Ajji Urmila see Yamini's progress over the week?
qa.a: She would likely feel pleased and amused, seeing her move from jumbled numbers to spotting "more" at a glance.

grounding: Shows a young child moving from jumbled counting to one-by-one counting to comparing which plate has more.

passage: Black clouds rolled over the village, and Ramesh had to get the hens into the coop before the storm. "Count them in, Mohit!" His son, five, stood at the little door. "One, two, three…" The first drops fell. Hens ran in, flapping. "…seven, eight." Mohit frowned. "Papa, we have nine. One is less!" Ramesh looked round and found the brown hen under the cart. Mohit counted again. "Nine! All here."

qa.q: How many hens should there have been?
qa.a: Nine.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling when he said "One is less!"?
qa.a: He was worried that a hen was missing and wanted his father to find it before the rain.

qa.q: How could Ramesh make the most of Mohit's counting?
qa.a: Give him the counting job every evening and thank him when his count catches a missing hen.

qa.q: What would change if Mohit hadn't counted?
qa.a: The brown hen might have been left out in the storm without anyone noticing.

grounding: Shows a young child counting hens under time pressure and noticing when there is one less.

passage: In their Chennai flat, Kunal, five, and his little brother Siddharth each got a bowl of grapes. Kunal peered into both. "His has more!" "They're the same," said their mother. Kunal tipped his own onto the table and counted: "One, two… eleven." Then he counted Siddharth's. "Eleven." He looked puzzled. "But his bowl looks full." "His bowl is smaller," said their mother. Kunal put his grapes back and said, "Same. Okay."

qa.q: How many grapes did Kunal count in his own bowl?
qa.a: Eleven.

qa.q: Why did Kunal look puzzled after counting?
qa.a: He expected Siddharth to have more, so finding the same number confused him.

qa.q: How could their mother help Kunal next time he thinks something is unfair?
qa.a: Encourage him to count again, as he did, so he can check "more" and "less" for himself.

qa.q: What is it like for Siddharth when Kunal says his has more?
qa.a: He might feel worried his grapes could be taken, and relieved when the count shows they are the same.

grounding: Shows a young child using counting to check whether a bowl really holds more.

passage: I'm Naveen, Ojas's older brother. Yesterday it was too hot to go out, so Ojas, who is five, emptied Amma's kitchen drawer onto the floor. The steel colander went on his head: "My space helmet." The rolling pin became a rocket, then a telescope, then a microphone for a song about Mars. A ladle was a moon digger. I only wanted to watch cartoons, but I ended up being mission control. I can't tell what's in his head, but he never ran out of ideas.

qa.q: What did Ojas put on his head?
qa.a: The steel colander.

qa.q: What does Ojas turning the rolling pin into three things suggest?
qa.a: He was deeply absorbed and enjoying the game, full of excitement about his next idea.

qa.q: How could Amma support this kind of play at home?
qa.a: Keep a box of safe, ordinary objects he can use freely, and ask "What else could it be?"

qa.q: How does Naveen feel about being pulled into the game?
qa.a: He didn't plan to play, but seems to enjoy being mission control once he joins in.

grounding: Shows a young child inventing many new uses for kitchen objects in a space game, seen by an older brother.

passage: Monday: a fridge arrived at the flat, and Ujjwal, five, claimed the box. He cut two holes and called it a car. His mother Alka drew headlights. Wednesday: the box lay on its side. "It's a boat now," he said, rowing with a broom handle. "The floor is the sea." Saturday: he had cut a window and a door. "It's my shop. I'm selling stones." He charged Alka two leaves for a round pebble.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal call the box on Monday?
qa.a: A car.

qa.q: What might Ujjwal have felt when he turned the box into a shop?
qa.a: He seemed proud and excited to have a new idea for the same box.

qa.q: How could Alka support Ujjwal's ideas without taking over?
qa.a: Join in on his terms, like paying with leaves, and let him decide what the box becomes next.

qa.q: What would change if Alka had thrown the box away on Monday?
qa.a: Ujjwal would lose the chance to keep reinventing it, which is where his best ideas came from.

grounding: Shows a young child finding new uses for the same box across a week.

passage: The power went out in the evening storm, and the fan stopped. Uma, five, sat in the dark with her father Raghav and one torch. "I'm bored," she said. Then she shone the torch on the wall and made her hand into a crocodile. "Papa, do a bird." He did. She held a steel plate in front of the light: "Look, the moon!" By the time the power came back, their wall had a whole zoo and a moon, and Uma didn't want the lights on.

qa.q: What did Uma hold in front of the light to make the moon?
qa.a: A steel plate.

qa.q: How did Uma feel at first, and what changed?
qa.a: She felt bored in the dark at first, then became excited and happy as she invented the shadow zoo.

qa.q: What did Raghav do that helped the game grow?
qa.a: He joined in when she asked for a bird, so her idea could build into a whole zoo.

qa.q: What would change if the power had come back right away?
qa.a: Uma might never have found her game, since the dark and the torch sparked the idea.

grounding: Shows a young child turning a torch and a plate into a shadow zoo and moon during a power cut.

passage: In a Madrid schoolyard, Javier, five, was playing tag with Jin. Every time he tagged her, he grabbed her whole arm and nearly pulled them both over. "Too hard," Jin said. "Just touch." Javier stopped. Next time he reached out, tapped her shoulder with two fingers, and ran the other way, arms out for balance as he turned. Jin laughed and chased him. At the end of the game he stood an arm's length away to say bye.

qa.q: What did Jin tell Javier to do instead of grabbing?
qa.a: "Just touch."

qa.q: What might Javier have felt when Jin said "Too hard"?
qa.a: He may have felt a bit surprised or sorry, but he took it seriously and changed straight away.

qa.q: How could a teacher support what Javier learned?
qa.a: Praise him for listening and practise "gentle tag" with the whole group.

qa.q: How might Jin feel when Javier taps her with two fingers?
qa.a: Relieved and respected, and happy to keep playing with him.

grounding: Shows a young child learning to keep his tag gentle and respect a peer's body while staying balanced in the game.

passage: In the school's PE period, Madhuri, the teacher, gave each child a hula hoop. "Stand in your bubble. Move around without popping anyone else's." Deepika, five, walked, then skipped, carefully keeping her hoop from bumping others. When her friend dropped his hoop and she ran to hug him, he stepped back. "No hug." Deepika froze, then nodded. "Okay. High five?" He smiled and held up his hand.

qa.q: What did Madhuri give each child?
qa.a: A hula hoop.

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling when she froze after "No hug"?
qa.a: She was probably surprised and a little hurt, but she accepted his choice.

qa.q: Which choice by Deepika worked, and why?
qa.a: Offering a high five instead, because it kept the friendship warm while respecting his wish.

qa.q: How does Deepika's friend experience her response?
qa.a: He feels his "no" was respected, which makes him happy to connect in another way.

grounding: Shows a young child keeping to her own space in a movement game and respecting a friend's body boundary.

passage: I'm Ramesh, the watchman at the apartment gate. Every evening I see the children playing stuck-in-the-mud. Madhuri, five, is fast and good at dodging without bumping into anyone. Yesterday, when she freed a boy, he said, "Stop, you're pulling my shirt." She let go straight away and stepped back. She didn't argue. After that she just tapped his hand. I can't know what she thought, but the game went on without a fight.

qa.q: What game do the children play every evening?
qa.a: Stuck-in-the-mud.

qa.q: What might Madhuri have felt when the boy said "Stop"?
qa.a: Maybe a little embarrassed, but she seemed to care about his comfort, since she let go straight away without arguing.

qa.q: How could the children's parents build on this?
qa.a: Tell Madhuri they noticed she stopped when asked, and remind all the children that "stop" means stop.

qa.q: How does Ramesh see Madhuri's reaction?
qa.a: Ramesh sees she respected the boy's wish quickly, while admitting nobody can know her thoughts.

grounding: Shows a young child dodging with good balance and stopping when a peer says she is pulling, seen by a watchman.

passage: Every morning the milk can went from their house to the village dairy, and every morning Sarika carried it. Today her little brother Darshan, five, said, "I'll do it." Sarika walked beside him. He held the can with both hands, stopping twice to rest, and didn't spill a drop. At the dairy counter he lifted it up himself. On the way home he walked in front, chest out, waving at every neighbour.

qa.q: Who usually carried the milk can?
qa.a: Sarika carried it every morning.

qa.q: What does Darshan walking in front with his chest out suggest?
qa.a: He felt proud and grown-up after carrying the can all the way without spilling.

qa.q: How could Sarika help Darshan keep this good feeling?
qa.a: Let him carry the can again and tell the family what he managed, praising his effort.

qa.q: What is it like for Sarika to walk beside him instead of carrying the can?
qa.a: She may feel a bit anxious watching, but also glad and proud to see him manage.

grounding: Shows a young child standing taller with pride after carrying the milk can himself.

passage: In the park in Lyon, Amara, five, wobbled on her bike without the little side wheels. Her grandmother Ines jogged behind, holding the seat. "Let go? Don't let go!" Ines let go. Amara didn't notice for three long pedals. Then she did, squeaked, and kept going all the way to the fountain. She braked, turned round, and put both hands on her hips. "Grand-mère! I did it by myself!"

qa.q: Where did Amara ride to without help?
qa.a: All the way to the fountain.

qa.q: What does Amara putting both hands on her hips suggest?
qa.a: She felt proud and pleased with herself for riding alone.

qa.q: How could Ines respond to make the moment count?
qa.a: Celebrate the effort, like "you kept pedalling even when you noticed", not just the result.

qa.q: What was it like for Ines to let go of the seat?
qa.a: It was likely a nervous moment, followed by relief and joy when Amara kept going.

grounding: Shows a young child's pride after riding a bike alone for the first time.

passage: In the kindergarten, Seema, the class teacher, came round to look at the drawings. Shreya, five, had drawn her family under a big sun. At the bottom, in wobbly capital letters, she had written SHREYA. It was the first time she'd written her whole name without looking at the card. "Did you do this by yourself?" Seema asked. Shreya nodded, sat up very straight, and later asked to show it to the principal.

qa.q: What did Shreya write at the bottom of her drawing?
qa.a: She wrote SHREYA in wobbly capital letters.

qa.q: What does Shreya sitting up very straight suggest?
qa.a: She felt proud of writing her whole name by herself for the first time.

qa.q: How could Seema support Shreya's pride in this achievement?
qa.a: Let her take it to the principal and put it on the wall, praising the effort she put in.

qa.q: How might the principal see Shreya's visit?
qa.a: The principal would likely feel pleased and warm, seeing a small child so proud of her work.

grounding: Shows a young child's pride after writing her name alone for the first time.

passage:
Teacher's note, Vijay, Friday
At story time I asked Dhruv (5) to read the word on the card. He couldn't, and one child laughed. Dhruv put his head on his knees and whispered, "I'm stupid. I'm always bad." He didn't want to come to snack. I sat beside him and said, "You don't know this word yet. That's all." Later we read it together. I've spoken to the child who laughed and will tell Dhruv's parents what he said, so they can reassure him too.

qa.q: What did Vijay ask Dhruv to read?
qa.a: The word on the card.

qa.q: What does Dhruv whispering "I'm stupid" suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and bad about himself as a whole, not just about one word.

qa.q: Which part of Vijay's response helped, and why?
qa.a: Saying "You don't know this word yet" helped, because it separated one mistake from Dhruv himself.

qa.q: How might Dhruv's parents feel when Vijay tells them?
qa.a: They may feel worried and sad, and want to reassure him that he isn't bad or stupid.

grounding: Shows a young child feeling bad about himself after failing in front of others, and his teacher responding.

passage: Dilnaz, five, had begged to carry the eggs home from the village shop. Halfway there she tripped, and three cracked on the road. At the gate her grandmother sighed, "Big girls don't drop things." Dilnaz ran behind the haystack and hid her face. "I'm bad at everything," she told her cousin Ujjwal when he found her. He sat down beside her. "You carried nine eggs. You dropped three. That's not everything." She peeked at him through her fingers.

qa.q: How many eggs cracked on the road?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: Why did Dilnaz say "I'm bad at everything"?
qa.a: She felt deeply ashamed after dropping the eggs and her grandmother's comment made her feel bad about herself as a whole.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal do that helped, and why?
qa.a: He stayed with her and pointed out what she did well, which helped her see one slip as small.

qa.q: What would change if her grandmother had said "Accidents happen" instead?
qa.a: Dilnaz would probably feel sorry about the eggs but not so bad about herself.

grounding: Shows a young child feeling bad about herself after failing an adult's expectation, and a cousin gently reframing it.

passage: At the spring concert in a Montreal school, Nour, five, forgot her one line. The audience waited. She stood frozen, then ran off the stage and hid behind the curtain. Her teacher Yuki found her crouched there. "I'm bad," Nour said into her knees. "I ruin things." Yuki knelt. "You forgot a line. Everyone does. You're not bad." She held out her hand. "Want to stand with me and wave at the end?" Nour took it.

qa.q: Where did Nour hide after forgetting her line?
qa.a: Behind the curtain.

qa.q: What does Nour saying "I ruin things" suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and worthless, blaming her whole self for one forgotten line.

qa.q: What worked in Yuki's response, and why?
qa.a: Naming the mistake as normal and offering a small way back, waving at the end, helped Nour rejoin without pressure.

qa.q: What is it like for Yuki to find Nour crouched behind the curtain?
qa.a: She probably feels concerned and tender, wanting Nour to know one slip doesn't define her.

grounding: Shows a young child feeling fundamentally bad after forgetting her line in front of others, and a teacher's caring response.

passage: Tarun had spent all afternoon shaping a clay pot for the village school fair. While he was out, his sister Arohi, five, picked it up to look and dropped it. The rim cracked. She put it back, turned the crack to the wall, and went to sit on the step, twisting her dupatta. When Tarun came back she jumped up. "I broke it. I'm sorry. I held it and it fell." She held out her own clay. "You can have mine to fix it."

qa.q: What did Tarun make for the village school fair?
qa.a: A clay pot.

qa.q: Why did Arohi twist her dupatta on the step?
qa.a: She felt guilty about cracking the pot and was nervous about telling Tarun.

qa.q: What would you advise Tarun to say to Arohi?
qa.a: He could thank her for telling the truth and let her help fix it, even if he feels upset.

qa.q: How might Tarun feel when Arohi confesses?
qa.a: Upset about the pot, but perhaps softer because she told him herself and offered her clay.

grounding: Shows a young child recognising she broke her brother's pot, feeling sorry and owning up.

passage: At the playground in Cape Town, Lindiwe, five, wanted the swing, so she pushed Noa off it. Noa fell on the gravel and her knee started to bleed. Lindiwe stared at the red scrape. Her face crumpled. "I didn't mean it to bleed," she whispered. She ran to the teacher, then came back and stood beside Noa while the teacher cleaned the knee. "Sorry I pushed you. You can have the swing." She held Noa's hand the whole time.

qa.q: Where did Noa fall?
qa.a: On the gravel.

qa.q: What does Lindiwe's crumpled face suggest?
qa.a: She felt guilty and sorry when she saw the scrape, realising her push had hurt Noa.

qa.q: What small step could Lindiwe try next time she wants the swing?
qa.a: Ask for a turn or wait, instead of pushing.

qa.q: How might Noa see Lindiwe's apology?
qa.a: Noa may still be hurt and cross, but feel comforted that Lindiwe stayed, said sorry and held her hand.

grounding: Shows a young child recognising she hurt a friend by pushing, feeling remorse and trying to make amends.

passage: In class, Nazia, five, was cross that Kashish had taken the last glitter pen, so she scribbled a black line across Kashish's drawing. Kashish cried. Nazia went back to her seat and didn't touch her own drawing. At snack she didn't eat. Then she walked to the teacher's desk. "I spoiled Kashish's picture. On purpose." The teacher asked what she could do. Nazia went to Kashish and held out her own drawing. "You can have mine. Sorry."

qa.q: What did Nazia do to Kashish's drawing?
qa.a: She scribbled a black line across it.

qa.q: What does Nazia not eating at snack suggest?
qa.a: She felt guilty and bad about what she did, and it stayed on her mind.

qa.q: How could the teacher help Nazia after her confession?
qa.a: Thank her for telling the truth and help her find ways to handle being cross without spoiling others' work.

qa.q: How might Kashish feel when Nazia offers her own drawing?
qa.a: Still sad about her picture, but touched that Nazia said sorry and gave something of her own.

grounding: Shows a young child recognising her specific wrong, feeling remorse and trying to make it right.

passage: It was Priscila's fifth birthday, and her aunt Astrid had taken her to a café in Stockholm. Suddenly the waiter came out with a cake and a sparkler, and the whole café started singing. Everyone turned to look. Priscila slid down in her seat and pulled her hood over her face. When the song ended, people clapped. She peeked out, cheeks hot, and whispered, "Can we go home now?" Astrid squeezed her hand. "We can eat the cake first, quietly."

qa.q: What did the waiter bring out?
qa.a: A cake and a sparkler.

qa.q: Why did Priscila pull her hood over her face?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and overwhelmed by everyone suddenly looking at her.

qa.q: What could Astrid do next time to make a celebration easier for Priscila?
qa.a: Ask her beforehand if she wants a song, or keep it just between the two of them.

qa.q: How might Astrid feel when Priscila asks to go home?
qa.a: A little sorry the surprise went wrong, and keen to make the rest of the treat calm for her.

grounding: Shows a young child's sudden self-consciousness when a whole café sings at her.

passage: At the school assembly, the principal called out, "Kiran, from UKG, please come up! He found a lost wallet and gave it to the office." Kiran, five, walked up the steps. Three hundred faces looked at him. The microphone squealed. He stared at his shoes, his ears going red, and he didn't say a word. Sachin, his class teacher, came up and stood beside him until the clapping stopped, then walked him back to his line.

qa.q: What had Kiran found?
qa.a: A lost wallet.

qa.q: What does Kiran staring at his shoes with red ears suggest?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and overwhelmed by so many people looking at him, even though it was praise.

qa.q: How could Sachin support Kiran after the assembly?
qa.a: Tell Kiran quietly how proud the class is of him, and ask if he'd prefer praise in class next time.

qa.q: How might the principal see Kiran's silence?
qa.a: The principal might read it as shyness and could learn that some children prefer quieter praise.

grounding: Shows a young child's embarrassment at unwanted attention during public praise.

passage: I'm Himani, Ganga's older sister. At our cousin's wedding, Ganga, who is five, danced in the middle of the floor. Then the aunties noticed. "Look at her! So cute!" They pinched her cheeks, took photos, asked her to dance again. Ganga stopped moving, grabbed my kurta and hid behind my legs. One uncle kept saying, "Dance, na!" She shook her head and pressed her face into my back. I don't know exactly what she felt, but she didn't dance again that night.

qa.q: Who pinched Ganga's cheeks at the wedding?
qa.a: The aunties.

qa.q: What might Ganga have felt when everyone started watching her?
qa.a: She likely felt embarrassed and overwhelmed by all the sudden attention.

qa.q: How could Himani help Ganga in that moment?
qa.a: Stay with her, gently tell the relatives she needs a break, and let her choose whether to dance again.

qa.q: How does Himani see Ganga's change on the dance floor?
qa.a: Himani notices she went from dancing freely to hiding, but only guesses at the feeling.

grounding: Shows a young child's self-consciousness when relatives crowd round her, seen by an older sister.

passage: On a hot afternoon in Berlin, Jamal's ice cream fell off the cone and landed on the pavement with a splat. Jamal, five, just stood there, his mouth open, and then started to cry. Nadia, his friend from next door, stopped licking hers. Her face fell too. She looked at her cone, then at him, and held it out. "You can have some of mine." Jamal took one lick, sniffed, and gave it back.

qa.q: Where did Jamal's ice cream land?
qa.a: On the pavement.

qa.q: What does Nadia's face falling suggest?
qa.a: She felt sad and sorry for Jamal when she saw him crying.

qa.q: How could a parent nearby support Nadia's kindness?
qa.a: Notice it and thank her, and help sort out another ice cream if possible.

qa.q: What is it like for Jamal when Nadia offers her ice cream?
qa.a: It probably comforts him to see someone cares, even if he only takes one lick.

grounding: Shows a young child feeling sorrow at a friend's distress and offering to share.

passage: On the first day of term, a new girl in the kindergarten cried for her mother by the door. Most children kept playing. Raghav, five, stopped building and watched her. His mouth turned down. After a minute he went to Vinita, the teacher, and tugged her sleeve. "She's sad. She misses her mummy." Vinita went over. Raghav followed and stood near the girl, holding out his toy car.

qa.q: Who was crying by the door?
qa.a: A new girl in the kindergarten.

qa.q: What does Raghav's mouth turning down suggest?
qa.a: He felt sad and concerned when he saw the girl crying.

qa.q: How could Vinita encourage Raghav's concern?
qa.a: Thank him for noticing and let him stay near the new girl as a friendly face.

qa.q: How might the new girl feel when Raghav holds out his car?
qa.a: She may feel a little less alone, seeing someone cares.

grounding: Shows a young child feeling concern at a new classmate's distress and getting help.

passage: I'm Tanuja, Bhavna's mother's friend. We were walking to the market in the rain when Bhavna, who is five, saw an old man drop his bag of tomatoes in the puddle. He bent down slowly, groaning. Bhavna stopped and stared, her lip trembling. "Amma, he's sad," she said. Her mother helped him gather them, and Bhavna picked up two tomatoes and held them out to him. I can't know all she felt, but she kept looking back at him as we left.

qa.q: What did the old man drop in the puddle?
qa.a: His bag of tomatoes.

qa.q: What does Bhavna's trembling lip suggest?
qa.a: She felt sad and sorry for the old man when she saw him struggle.

qa.q: How could Bhavna's mother build on this moment later?
qa.a: Talk with her about what she noticed and tell her helping him was kind.

qa.q: What might the old man feel when Bhavna holds out the tomatoes?
qa.a: He might feel touched and grateful that a small child noticed and helped.

grounding: Shows a young child feeling sorrow at an old man's distress, seen by a family friend.

passage: In their kitchen in Oslo, Ines, the grandmother, caught her finger in the drawer and gasped. Anders, five, looked up from his puzzle. Ines was holding her hand and wincing. Anders came over and looked at her finger very seriously. Then he ran to his room and came back with his teddy. "Teddy makes it better." He patted her arm, the way she did for him. "Does it hurt still?" Ines smiled. "A little less now."

qa.q: What did Anders bring back from his room?
qa.a: His teddy.

qa.q: Why did Anders bring his teddy to Ines?
qa.a: He was worried about her pain and wanted to comfort her the way he gets comforted.

qa.q: How could Ines show Anders his comfort mattered?
qa.a: Thank him, hold the teddy for a moment and tell him it helped.

qa.q: What is it like for Ines to be comforted by her grandson?
qa.a: It likely feels touching and funny, and it softens the pain a little.

grounding: Shows a young child noticing his grandmother's pain and offering simple comfort.

passage: At kindergarten playtime, a boy tripped on the step and scraped his elbow. He sat crying. Jasleen, five, ran over first. She crouched down and looked at the scrape, her forehead wrinkled. "Ouch," she said softly. Then she fetched a wet tissue from the tap and dabbed at it. When Vinita, the teacher, came, Jasleen said, "I'm helping," and held his hand while Vinita cleaned it properly.

qa.q: What did Jasleen fetch from the tap?
qa.a: A wet tissue.

qa.q: What does Jasleen's wrinkled forehead suggest?
qa.a: She felt worried and concerned about the boy's hurt elbow.

qa.q: How could Vinita respond to Jasleen's helping?
qa.a: Thank her for caring and show her that getting a grown-up is the best first step next time.

qa.q: How might the boy feel with Jasleen holding his hand?
qa.a: Comforted and less alone while his elbow is cleaned.

grounding: Shows a young child noticing a classmate's pain and offering simple comfort.

passage: I'm Pallavi, from the flat upstairs. Yesterday I was visiting when Samir's baby sister bumped her head on the table and began to wail. Samir, who's five, dropped his crayons and crawled over. He looked at the red mark, then kissed it very carefully. Then he sang her the song their mother sings at bedtime, out of tune. She stopped crying to stare at him. I don't know what he felt, but he didn't go back to his drawing until she smiled.

qa.q: What did Samir do after looking at the red mark?
qa.a: He kissed it very carefully.

qa.q: What might Samir have been feeling when his sister wailed?
qa.a: He seemed worried and upset for her, which is why he came straight over.

qa.q: How could Samir's parents encourage his care?
qa.a: Tell him they noticed how he comforted her and that his song helped.

qa.q: How does Pallavi see Samir's comforting?
qa.a: Pallavi is touched by it but admits it's only a guess what he felt.

grounding: Shows a young child noticing his baby sister's hurt and comforting her, seen by a neighbour.

passage: At the sports club's under-six race, Saurabh came fourth. He stamped his foot and threw his cap on the grass. "Not fair!" Coach Amandeep knelt beside him. "You're cross. Big breath with me?" They breathed in and out together, twice. Saurabh picked up his cap. When the winner walked past, he mumbled, "Well done." Then he asked, "Can I race again next week?"

qa.q: What place did Saurabh come in the race?
